papers.title_in_file: A quantum graph approach to metamaterial design
papers.version_note: The text layer is the Scientific Reports 2022 published version (volume 12, article 18006, received 7 July 2022, accepted 12 October 2022); the file name and record id carry 2023 and arXiv 2306.05890.
papers.what_it_is: A theory and numerical-demonstration paper that models a 2D metamaterial as an infinite square periodic quantum graph with open-graph resonators at the vertices, and computes band diagrams, Gaussian beam refraction at one interface and an N layer transfer matrix.
papers.why_not: The paper uses quantum graph scattering theory as a classical wave model of metamaterials; it has no quantum computing or machine learning workload and no fraud, finance or evaluation content. Entries below are filed under method as the modelling approach.

assertions.value: The authors state that the metamaterial is modeled as an infinite square periodic quantum graph embedded in a 2D real space, with a single resonant element modelled as an open quantum graph that is then periodically arranged.
assertions.anchor: Introduction and Section 'Waves in finite open quantum graphs', p.2
quotes: the metamaterial is modeled as an infinite square periodic quantum graph embedded in a 2D real space.
we can model a single resonant element as an open quantum graph, which is then periodically arranged to construct the metamaterial.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own model set-up in the Introduction and in the resonator section.

assertions.value: The authors state that the mapping from incoming to outgoing wave amplitudes at the vertices is described by a unitary matrix, and that they assume Neumann boundary conditions at individual vertices, enforcing wave continuity and flux conservation.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Waves in finite open quantum graphs', p.3
quotes: the mapping from all incoming to all outgoing wave amplitudes at the vertices is described by a unitary matrix
We assume Neumann boundary conditions at individual vertices enforcing wave continuity and flux conservation at each
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its vertex model in the resonator section.
assertions.reader_inference: A unitary vertex matrix means the model has no loss or absorption; the paper does not discuss loss.

assertions.value: The authors give the scattering matrix of a connected open graph, reducing it to a single scatterer, as SˆŴ(k) = SˆLL + SˆLE Iˆ − Pˆ (k)SˆEE −1Pˆ (k)SˆEL, built from prompt lead reflections, lead to edge coupling, edge propagation and edge to lead coupling.
assertions.anchor: Eq. (6), Section 'Waves in finite open quantum graphs', p.3
quotes: SˆŴ(k) = SˆLL + SˆLE Iˆ − Pˆ (k)SˆEE −1Pˆ (k)SˆEL,
reducing the entire connected graph in Ŵ(V , E, L) to a single scatterer illustrated in Fig. 2.
assertions.certainty_reason: The text points to Kottos and Smilansky for details; the derivation is not given in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The expression is the standard graph scattering formula attributed to reference 17 in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that Bloch's theorem relates the solution in any unit cell to the solution at the central vertex, and that the wave vector k on each edge and the quasi-wave vectors fulfill the secular equation det Iˆ − eiklBˆ (κx, κy)SˆŴ(k) = 0.
assertions.anchor: Eq. (11) and Eq. (15), Section 'A quantum graph model for a metamaterial', pp.4-5
quotes: we can use Bloch’s theorem to describe the wave solution in any unit cell nm in terms of the solution at the central vertex
which is satisfied if the wave vector k on each edge and the quasi-wave vectors κx and κy fulfill the secular equation
det Iˆ − eiklBˆ (κx, κy)SˆŴ(k) = 0.
assertions.certainty_reason: The condition is stated as the paper's dispersion condition, derived in the text from Eqs. (9), (10) and (12).

assertions.value: The authors state that real or imaginary solutions of the Bloch wave number correspond to propagating or evanescent waves respectively, the latter occurring in band gaps.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Wave solutions for the infinite lattice', p.5
quotes: We encounter real or imaginary solutions of κx(k, κy) corresponding to propagating or evanescent waves, respectively, the latter occurring in band gaps.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement of how the paper interprets its dispersion solutions.

assertions.value: For a lattice without resonators, where each edge is directly connected through a point-scatterer vertex, the authors give the dispersion relation 2 cos (kl) = cos (κxl) + cos (κyl).
assertions.anchor: Eq. (18), Section 'Wave propagation in metamaterials, plane wave solutions', p.5
quotes: we consider a lattice without resonators where each edge is directly connected through the vertex.
2 cos (kl) = cos (κxl) + cos (κyl).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the result 'by solving Eq. (15)' without showing the algebra, so the derivation is not quotable.

assertions.anchor: Sections on plane wave solutions and Gaussian beams, pp.5-6
quotes: energy flow is given by the Poynting vector J = (Jx, Jy)T normal to the iso-frequency contour.
Plane wave solutions travel in the direction of the wave vector κ , which does not necessarily agree with the direction of energy flow given by the Poynting
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its energy flow direction this way in the plane wave section.

assertions.value: The authors give the one dimensional flux of the wave function on edge p as k times the difference between the squared magnitudes of the outgoing and incoming amplitudes on that edge.
quotes: The 1D flux J of the wave function ψnm
assertions.certainty_reason: The flux is the paper's own definition used to build the Poynting vector.

assertions.value: The authors construct a Gaussian beam by Fourier expansion over the eigenfunctions on the iso-frequency contour, with the beam width and a phase factor setting the width and tilt of the beam; solutions outside the contour are evanescent and contribute nothing in the far field. Space on the graph is discretised, so the spatial integrals are too.
assertions.anchor: Eqs. (22) to (24), Section 'Wave propagation in metamaterials, Gaussian beams', pp.6-7
quotes: Solutions outside are evanescent and so contribute nothing in the far field.
We chose the beam profile to be Gaussian
determines the tilt angle of the beam with respect to the horizontal axis of the lattice.
Since the space on the graph is discretised, so too are the spacial integrals.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its beam construction and discretisation as method set-up.

assertions.value: The authors report that varying the phase modulation across each resonant element in only one dimension breaks the symmetry of the scattering and gives a saddle shaped band, which they state can be exploited for negative refraction; the figure caption gives lx = 1 and ly = 1 for the symmetric case and lx = 0 and ly = 1 for the asymmetric case.
assertions.anchor: Eq. (25), Fig. 7, Section 'Band engineering', p.8
quotes: varying the phase modulation across each resonant element only in one dimension breaks the symmetry of the scattering and gives rise to a saddle shaped band, which can be exploited to yield negative refraction
Plot (b) is for lx = 1 , ly = 1 . Plot (c) is for lx = 0 , ly = 1.
assertions.certainty_reason: A numerical band diagram for one resonator design, shown only as a figure; the text gives no further quantitative detail.
assertions.reader_inference: The result is for a single cross resonator family at the parameter values named in the caption.

assertions.value: The authors state that the two materials share the single value of k and the Bloch phase tangential to the interface, giving the boundary condition that the tangential Bloch wave numbers of material 1 and 2 are equal; the wave vectors normal to the interface follow from the dispersion curve of each material.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Wave refraction between metamaterials', pp.8-9
quotes: enforcing k1 = k2 := k
leading to the boundary condition κ1,y = κ2,y := κy
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states these as the boundary conditions of its interface model.

assertions.value: The authors state that with the eigenfunctions rescaled so the horizontal flux magnitude of each component is equal, flux conservation across the interface reduces to |A1|2 + |B2|2 = |B1|2 + |A2|2, meaning the sum of the squared magnitudes of A1 and B2 equals that of B1 and A2, so interface scattering is described as a unitary process.
quotes: we rescale the eigenfunction solutions of each material such that the magnitude of the horizontal flux of each component is equal
and wave scattering at the interface can then be described in terms of a unitary scattering process.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated in the interface section as following from the flux scaling choice; the scaling assumes real normal Bloch wave numbers (propagating waves), which the paper notes next to Eq. (29).
assertions.reader_inference: The unitarity holds for propagating (real normal wave number) channels; the paper does not treat evanescent channels at the interface.

assertions.value: The authors define the interface scattering matrix by two events: event I is a wave incident from material 1 onto material 2 with amplitude A1 = 1 and B2 = 0, and event II is a wave incident from material 2 onto material 1 with amplitude B2 = 1 and A1 = 0, each giving a reflected and a transmitted amplitude.
quotes: Event I describes a wave incident from material 1 onto material 2 with amplitude A1 = 1 and B2 = 0
Event II describes a wave incident from material 2 onto material 1 with amplitude B2 = 1 and A1 = 0
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its interface scattering matrix by these two events.

assertions.value: The authors show, as numerical figures, a Gaussian beam incident from material 1 with amplitude A1 = 1 and no incident beam from material 2, with B2 = 0, onto an interface, with beam focal point n′ = −60 and tilt κy′ = 1/l; with the saddle shaped band material on the right they report the reflection and transmission behaviour of Fig. 11. The text gives no numerical refraction angles or coefficients.
assertions.anchor: Eq. (40), Figs. 10 and 11, p.10 and p.11
quotes: The results of this unitary interface scattering is shown in Fig. 10 for a Gaussian beam incident from material 1 with amplitude A1 = 1 and no incident beam from material 2, that is, B2 = 0.
The expansion coefficients α−60 are as in Eq. (23) for a beam focal point n′ = −60 and tilt given by κy′ = 1/l.
one obtains the reflection/transmission behaviour shown in Fig. 11.
assertions.certainty_reason: A single numerical run shown as a figure; the results are in the images, not the text.
assertions.reader_inference: The negative refraction and beam steering named in the abstract rest on these figures; the text layer holds no numbers for them.

assertions.value: The authors state that the coefficients for N layered metamaterials are found by the Transfer Matrix Method, which expresses the wave amplitudes in material N in terms of those in material 1 and can be rearranged so the whole layered system acts as a single point scatterer.
assertions.anchor: Eqs. (41) to (46), Section 'Waves in N layered metamaterials', p.12
quotes: This is done by the Transfer Matrix
Having now formulated both scattering and propagation, one can express the wave amplitudes in material N in terms of the wave amplitudes in material 1.
such that the entire system of layered materials acts as a single point scatterer
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines its N layer formalism in this section.

assertions.value: The authors show a three layered example of three metamaterials whose scattering matrices are the point scatterer, the cross resonator with parameters 0 and 4.45, and the point scatterer again, at k = 1/l, with an incident wave of amplitude A1 = 1 from the first material and no incident wave from the last. The result is given only as a figure.
quotes: iso-frequency contours of three metamaterials with properties defined by scattering matrices
SˆŴcross (k; 0, 4.45) and SˆŴpoint for k = 1/l
assertions.certainty_reason: A single numerical illustration reported only in a figure.

assertions.value: The authors state that existing simulation techniques for metamaterials can be quite time consuming when setting up the models, let alone considering design modifications, and that simple and computationally cheap models are needed for proof of principle studies.
assertions.anchor: Introduction, pp.1-2
quotes: These simulation techniques can be quite time consuming when setting up the models, let alone considering design modifications
need for simple and computationally cheap models for proof of principle studies.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without a timing comparison in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports no runtime or cost measurement for its own method or for the finite element, boundary element or transmission line models.

assertions.value: The authors propose a graph based technique that they describe as allowing a fast and flexible way to test resonant element proposals embedded periodically within a 2D square lattice, and state that the computation reduces to low-dimensional matrix problems with the help of Bloch's theorem.
assertions.anchor: Conclusion, p.12
quotes: We propose here a graph based technique for designing metamaterials allowing for a fast and flexible way to test resonant element proposals embedded periodically within a 2D square lattice.
the computation can be reduced to low-dimensional matrix problems with the help of Bloch’s theorem.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim of speed and flexibility; no benchmark is reported.

assertions.value: The authors state that a generalisation to 3D is straightforward by adding additional edges and vertices in the extra dimension. The paper does not carry out a three dimensional calculation.
assertions.anchor: Introduction, p.2
quotes: A generalisation to 3D is straightforward by adding additional edges and vertices in the extra dimension.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim with no 3D result in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that further results modelling various special wave effects will be presented in forthcoming publications, and that the datasets and the code used for the study are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. The paper includes no public code or data link.
assertions.anchor: Conclusion p.12; Data availability and Code availability, p.13
quotes: Further results modelling various special wave effects will be presented in forthcoming publications.
The code used to generate the datasets shown in this study are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope limit and availability terms.

assertions.value: The authors attribute to Veselago the result that a material with both permittivity and permeability less than zero has a negative refractive index.
assertions.anchor: Introduction, p.1
quotes: Veselago showed that when a material has both permittivity and permeability less than zero, its refractive index would be negative.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to earlier work.

assertions.value: The authors attribute to Pendry the theoretical construction of a lens from an ideal lossless slab with a refractive index of n = −1 that could focus light perfectly and overcome the diffraction limit of a traditional lens.
assertions.anchor: Introduction, p.1
quotes: Showing, given an ideal lossless slab of material with a refractive index of n = −1 in a medium with equal and opposite refractive index, a lens can be theoretically constructed that could focus light
Crucially such a material could overcome the diffraction limit of a traditional lens.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to earlier work.
